issues.legal_issue: An aggrieved tenant may challenge measures to recover secured property before the debt recovery tribunal, but the Supreme Court may decide the merits of a long-pending appeal without first requiring resort to that remedy.
material_facts: The tenant challenged orders made in proceedings concerning possession under the secured-property recovery process.
A statutory appeal to the debt recovery tribunal was available to a tenant claiming under a borrower, and that tribunal could set aside the creditor’s action and restore the previous position.
The appeals had been pending before the Supreme Court since 2016.
issues.conclusion: An alternative remedy was available, but because the appeals had been pending for years, the Court examined the merits without directing the tenant to pursue that remedy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act provides an appeal to the debt recovery tribunal, including for a tenant claiming under a borrower. In Harshad Govardhan Sondagar v. International Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd., the Court recognised a tenant’s right of appeal; in Kanaiyalal Lalchand Sachdev v. State of Maharashtra, it held that the tribunal may set aside the secured creditor’s action and restore the status quo ante. The Court relied on the prolonged pendency of these appeals in deciding to consider the merits without requiring use of the alternative remedy.

predicates.secured_property_recovery_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning measures to recover possession of secured property.
predicates.alternative_tribunal_remedy_available: The aggrieved person has an available remedy before a tribunal that can review the recovery measure and grant effective relief.
predicates.appeal_pending_for_extended_period: The appeal has remained pending before the court for an extended period.

issues.definition: When a secured-property recovery appeal has remained pending for an extended period and an effective tribunal remedy is also available, the court may decide the merits without directing the appellant to use that remedy.

issues.legal_issue: A person claiming tenancy in secured property cannot prevent recovery of possession when the claimed tenancy is not credibly established, a claimed term exceeding one year lacks a registered instrument, or the claim otherwise fails the requirements applicable to the tenancy and recovery process.
material_facts: The appellant claimed an oral tenancy beginning before the mortgage and asserted that rent had been paid in advance for several years.
The supporting rent receipts were photocopies, and the earliest produced receipt was dated after the mortgage was created.
The borrowers did not identify a tenant in their detailed response to the recovery notice, and valuers had reported that the borrowers lived in the property.
The appellant claimed a tenancy extending for more than one year but produced no registered instrument.
The appellant was described as a tenant-in-sufferance, and no creditor consent had been sought for a purported renewal after the recovery notice.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not sufficiently establish a bona fide tenancy, and the appellant was not entitled to prevent the bank from taking possession. The claimed long-term tenancy was unsupported by a registered instrument; a tenant-in-sufferance could not rely on rent-law protection against the recovery process, and no creditor consent had been obtained for a purported post-notice renewal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, a lease for a term exceeding one year must be made by a registered instrument; Sections 65-A and 111 govern, respectively, certain leases created after a mortgage and determination of leases. Under Sections 13(2), 13(13), and 35 of the SARFAESI Act, the recovery process restricts post-notice dealings with secured property, and rent-law protection does not extend to a tenant-in-sufferance in conflict with that process. Harshad Govardhan Sondagar v. International Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. requires a registered instrument for a claimed term exceeding one year. Bajarang Shyamsunder Agarwal v. Central Bank of India holds that a valid tenancy predating the mortgage cannot be disturbed without lawful determination, that a tenancy created after the mortgage and before the recovery notice must satisfy the applicable transfer-of-property requirements, and that an unregistered instrument or oral agreement does not support possession beyond the legally prescribed period.

rule.if: secured_property_recovery_proceeding and (tenancy_not_credibly_proven or (claimed_term_exceeds_one_year and no_registered_lease) or tenant_in_sufferance or post_notice_renewal_without_creditor_consent)

predicates.secured_property_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a creditor's recovery of possession of property given as security.
predicates.tenancy_not_credibly_proven: The person claiming to be a tenant lacks reliable evidence establishing the claimed tenancy.
predicates.claimed_term_exceeds_one_year: The person claims a tenancy lasting more than one year.
predicates.no_registered_lease: No registered instrument supports the claimed tenancy for a term exceeding one year.
predicates.tenant_in_sufferance: The person in possession is a tenant-in-sufferance rather than a tenant with a valid subsisting tenancy.
predicates.post_notice_renewal_without_creditor_con: A tenancy is claimed to have been renewed after the recovery notice without the secured creditor's consent.

issues.definition: In a secured-property recovery proceeding, a tenant cannot prevent possession when the tenancy is not credibly proven, a claimed long-term tenancy lacks a registered lease, the person is a tenant-in-sufferance, or a claimed post-notice renewal lacks creditor consent.
